system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2138-07-28 12:27:00 to 2138-07-31 17:25:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure due to recurrent tracheal and bronchial stenosis from Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome and relapsing polychondritis. He presented with sudden shortness of breath and cyanosis at home, requiring EMS transport. He was stabilized with oxygen and nebulizers, then underwent bronchoscopy with balloon dilation of the trachea and bilateral mainstem bronchi, which improved his airway patency and oxygenation. His leukocytosis resolved without antibiotics, and pain was managed with oxycodone. He was restarted on home medications, including tobramycin nebulizers and Esbriet, with a new nebulizer provided. He was discharged home with follow-up planned in one month for repeat bronchoscopy and continued management of chronic conditions.
problems: Elevated white blood cell count, unspecified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're in the hospital because you were having trouble breathing and your oxygen levels were very low when you arrived.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I couldn’t catch my breath at home. It scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We put you on oxygen through your trach, and that helped. Your oxygen improved to 97% on 40% support. You’ve been having these episodes before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because of the narrowing in my airway from my condition. I was supposed to have a dilation soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we took you to the operating room today for a bronchoscopy. We found the same kind of narrowing in your trachea and left main bronchus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was it bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There was severe narrowing and some granulation tissue—scar-like growth—that’s common with your history. We used a balloon to stretch the areas open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. A chest X-ray afterward shows your left lung has re-expanded. That’s a good sign the airway is open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I still feel some pain when I breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. There was minor bleeding during the procedure, but we controlled it. You’ll be on pain meds like oxycodone every four hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is the infection they mentioned real?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: During the bronchoscopy, we saw pus, which means you had a post-obstructive pneumonia—basically, an infection behind the blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We started you on Zosyn, but Infectious Disease recommended switching to cefepime and flagyl. You’ll go home on levaquin for seven days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Levaquin? I’ve taken that before. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s generally well-tolerated. Some people get nausea or dizziness. Rarely, tendon issues. If you have severe pain, stop and call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on 40 mg of prednisone daily for three days, then tapering down over two weeks back to your usual 7.5 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. My rheumatologist usually has me on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your CT scan results. The airway narrowing is stable compared to before, which is good. But there’s a small area of inflammation in your left upper lobe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. It could be from the infection or from irritation during the procedure. There’s also a small bleed in the left bronchus, which is expected after biopsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that heal on its own?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s minor. We also saw a small fluid collection on the left side—likely reactive. Nothing to drain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. What about the bronchial wash results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The initial tests didn’t show bacteria or fungi. But the fungal culture later grew fusarium and penicillium—molds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not clear yet. These can be contaminants, but we’re sending more blood tests to check. You’ll see Infectious Disease soon to discuss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ll keep an eye out for fever or worsening cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Your white count was high at 13.1, but it’s likely from chronic inflammation, not a new infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had high counts before. My rheumatologist says it’s baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That matches what we’re seeing. Your kidney and liver labs are normal. You’re doing well on the current oxygen—we’re down to 30% now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I walk a bit today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the physical therapist will come by. Staying mobile helps prevent complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The Infectious Disease team reviewed your case. They agree the mold might not be active infection, but we’ll finish the levaquin and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pending blood tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re still pending. If they come back positive, we’ll adjust. But for now, no need for antifungal meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking really good. Oxygen saturation is 99% on the trach mask. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish all the levaquin. Follow the prednisone taper exactly—start with 40 mg daily for three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll write that down. And the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have oxycodone for three days. Take it only if needed, no more than every four hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know not to overuse it. What about my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—Esbriet, famotidine, losartan, calcium, and your nebulizers. Keep taking them as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rheumatology will see you soon. The pulmonary team will contact you about your next dilation. And call to schedule your Infectious Disease visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your discharge labs look excellent—white count is down to 7.0, and everything else is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get the paperwork ready. Remember: finish antibiotics, taper steroids, take pain meds only as needed, and keep all your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Call if you have trouble breathing, fever, or chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How’s your breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much easier. I’m on the trach mask and feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your exam shows clear thinking, good oxygen, and no distress. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team will call you to schedule your next bronchoscopy. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final reminder: if you feel short of breath, dizzy, or your trach needs suctioning more than usual, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I know the signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And keep your Narcan spray handy in case of accidental overdose, though you’re using the pain meds responsibly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve never had issues, but I’ll keep it close.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’re here if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for hypoxia and acute respiratory failure due to recurrent tracheal and left mainstem bronchus stenosis from ___ syndrome and relapsing polychondritis. He underwent bronchoscopy with balloon dilation, which improved airway patency and oxygenation. A post-obstructive pneumonia was identified during the procedure, and he was treated with intravenous antibiotics, later discharged on a 7-day course of levaquin. His leukocytosis was consistent with chronic inflammation. A CT scan showed stable airway narrowing, a small post-procedural bleed, and a new area of ground-glass opacity suspicious for early pneumonitis. Fungal cultures grew fusarium and penicillium species, prompting pending serologic testing and an outpatient ID follow-up. He was managed with a steroid taper, pain control, and continuation of home medications. He improved clinically, was weaned to trach mask, and discharged home with follow-up arranged.
